samples.text:
Nowadays many parents and teachers are discussing about whether young children should get homework or not. Some people think that homework in primary schools must be stopped because children needs time to play and rest. I mostly agree with this idea, although I think a small amount of homework can still be useful.

Firstly, primary school children are very young and they already spend six or seven hours in the classroom every day. When they come home they are tired and they want to play with their friends or watch cartoons. If they have to do a lot of homework, they can feel stressed and they may start to hate school. Also, playing is important for children because they learn how to share, how to solve problems and how to be creative. For example, when children play football in the park they learn teamwork, which is not possible from a worksheet.

Secondly, homework can make problem in the family. Many parents work until late and they don't have time to help their children. As a result, the child cannot finish the task or the parent do it for him, so the homework is not useful. In my country, I have seen many parents who argue with their children every evening because of homework.

However, some homework can be good. For example, reading a short story with parents for ten minutes is enjoyable and it improve the child's reading skill. This kind of activity is not same as difficult exercises.

In conclusion, I agree that most homework should be abolished in primary schools because children need to play and rest after school. But short and easy tasks like reading can still be given, because they help children without making them tired.
samples.why: Clear, largely consistent position · relevant ideas but examples are general and underdeveloped · mechanical linking (Firstly, Also, Secondly) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
It is often argued that primary school pupils should no longer be given homework, since young children need free time to play and recover after a long school day. While I accept that heavy workloads can be harmful at this age, I largely disagree with abolishing homework altogether, because short, well-designed tasks bring benefits that cannot easily be replaced.

There is certainly some truth in the argument for abolition. Young children have limited concentration, and after six hours of lessons many of them are simply too tired to learn effectively. Unstructured play is not a waste of time either; it helps children develop social skills, imagination and physical health. When homework takes up most of the evening, it can create anxiety and turn learning into a source of conflict between parents and children, which is clearly counterproductive.

However, the solution to excessive homework is to reduce it, not to remove it completely. A few minutes of daily reading or practising multiplication tables helps pupils to consolidate what they have learned in class, and a regular practice is particularly important for basic skills such as literacy and numeracy. Moreover, simple tasks teach children to organise their time and take responsibility for their own work, habits which will become essential at secondary school, where the workload increases sharply.

Homework can also strengthen the link between school and home. When parents see what their child is studying, they are better able to support them and to notice any difficulties at an early stage. A child who reads aloud to a parent each evening, for instance, is likely to gain confidence as well as fluency.

In conclusion, although young children certainly need time to play and rest, I do not believe homework should be abolished in primary schools. Instead, it should be limited to short, meaningful activities that support learning without taking over family life.
samples.why: Clear position maintained throughout · main ideas extended and supported, with some generalisation · logical paragraphing · good range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary · mostly error-free sentences.

samples.text:
The question of whether primary school children should be set homework has become increasingly contentious, with critics arguing that young pupils need their evenings for play and rest. I agree with this view to a considerable extent: formal homework offers limited academic benefit at this age, and the time it consumes is better spent on activities that support children's broader development. Nevertheless, I would stop short of banning all learning outside school.

The strongest case for abolition rests on how young children actually learn. At primary level, understanding is built largely through exploration, conversation and play rather than through repetitive written exercises. A seven-year-old who spends an evening building something with friends or helping to cook a meal is practising language, problem-solving and cooperation in a way that a worksheet rarely replicates. Rest matters just as much: tired children struggle to concentrate, and a school day followed by an hour of compulsory tasks can leave little room for the sleep and relaxation they need.

Homework also tends to widen existing inequalities. Pupils whose parents have the time and confidence to help them tend to complete assignments to a high standard, whereas those from busier or less advantaged households may fall behind or become discouraged. In such cases, what is intended as extra practice ends up rewarding family circumstances rather than effort, and can turn evenings into a source of tension.

That said, there is a difference between set homework and encouraging a love of learning at home. Reading together for pleasure, for example, is widely regarded as valuable and places little strain on children. Schools could therefore replace compulsory assignments with optional, informal suggestions of this kind.

Overall, I largely support abolishing formal homework in primary schools, since young children gain more from play, rest and family life. Informal reading at home, however, should still be warmly encouraged.
samples.why: Fully addresses the task with a nuanced, consistent position · well-developed, extended ideas · skilful paragraphing and cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary · wide range of structures with only a rare minor slip.
